summary: Reports on an experiment to review Proposed Standards and identify those that do not reflect practice in the world today. The result was a set of documents moved to Historic status. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A big spring cleaning of the rule book. People went through old rules nobody follows and moved them to a shelf marked old.

questions: how were obsolete rfcs reclassified as historic
what standards were moved to historic status
subtitle: The results of reclassifying obsolete Proposed Standards to Historic status.

tldr.problem: The IETF standards process requires periodic review of immature standards to retire those no longer in use, but this review has never been consistently done. Outdated Proposed Standards standards clog the catalog without clear guidance on which are obsolete.
tldr.mechanism: An experiment reviewed over 125 Proposed Standards with RFC numbers below 2000. Documents were assumed for retirement unless someone provided a reason to keep them. After discussion and objections, 61 documents were reclassified as Historic.
tldr.outcome: 61 Proposed Standards—including protocols for obsolete systems like AppleTalk and X.400, protocols never widely deployed like PEM and Whois++, and redundant Telnet options—were moved to Historic status to clean up the standards catalog.

facts.label: RFCs reviewed
facts.value: 125 Proposed Standards with RFC numbers under 2000

today: RFC 4450 is Informational. It documents the results of the experiment and recommends that the working group accept the results and mark the listed 61 standards as Historic. The process described here influenced how the IETF handles bulk retirement of obsolete standards going forward, though future efforts might be even more aggressive.

sections.title: The Standards Review Problem
sections.content: RFC 2026, the Internet Standards Process, calls for reviewing draft and proposed standards to decide whether to advance, retire, or revise them. However, this process was never consistently applied in the IETF's history. As a result, Proposed Standards that are no longer in use remain on the books with no clear indication of their status. Individual authors have had to write lengthy justification documents to retire single RFCs. By 2004, the community saw an opportunity to conduct a bulk experiment to identify and reclassify obsolete standards more efficiently.
sections.eli5: The rulebook said people should clean up old rules, but nobody did. So old rules nobody follows are still listed as official.

sections.title: How the Experiment Worked
sections.content: From Fall 2004 through Spring 2005, the authors conducted a bulk reclassification experiment. The procedure was conservative: assume each Proposed Standard with an RFC number below 2000 would be retired, then allow community members to remove it from the list if they provided a reason. A mailing list attracted 29 members who sent roughly 244 messages debating which documents should be kept. Documents were removed from retirement if they were known to be in active use, under ongoing revision, previously considered and rejected, or depended on by future work. The final list was presented to the IETF community and IESG for review before finalizing the reclassifications.
sections.eli5: They said, "These rules are old. Anything obsolete will be moved to the archive, but we'll listen if you say it's still used." People talked about which rules to keep, and some were saved.

sections.title: What Was Reclassified
sections.content: 61 Proposed Standards were moved to Historic status. They fall into several categories: multiprotocol extensions for systems now obsolete (AppleTalk, X.400, FDDI), protocols designed but never widely adopted (PEM for email security, Whois++ for directory services), and redundant Telnet terminal options from the early days of the Internet. Notably, some documents were removed during review: RFCs 1518 and 1519 (CIDR), 1381-1382, 1471-1473, 1582, 1598, and 1755 remained as standards because they were still in use, and RFC 1584 was kept due to expected future dependencies. The experiment concluded that some telnet options might eventually merit reconsideration but left open the question of whether to apply this process to draft standards and older RFCs.
sections.eli5: Instructions for talking to dead computer systems, protocols that never caught on, and old terminal features were moved to the archive. But some old rules that still work were kept.

sections.title: What the Results Showed
sections.content: The list of 61 reclassified documents revealed patterns: many were for protocols tied to obsolete platforms (such as SNA, IPX, AppleTalk, or X.400), while others were defined but never implemented at scale (such as PEM, the privacy-enhanced mail protocol, and Whois++). The community noted that more work was needed on some protocols: a discussion of deprecating a CIDR RFC, for example, actually spurred work on updates. The conservative parameters of the experiment meant some protocols that might be obsolete were kept because even one community member could defend them. The experience suggested that future cleanup might be even more aggressive or take into account different categories of old standards with different retirement criteria.
sections.eli5: Most of the old rules were for computers and networks that don't exist anymore. Some were never really used in the first place. The cleanup showed that some rules people thought were dead actually had small groups still using them.

references.text: Bradner, S., "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", BCP 9, RFC 2026, October 1996.
